name: Diagnostic_INT-SUB_1
questiontext:
Using the substitution \(u = \cos({{CT:0}})\) integrate {{CT:1}} with respect to {{CT:2}}.

[[input:ans1]]

[[validation:ans1]]
generalfeedback:
We are told to use the substitution \(u=\cos({{CT:0}})\), so we therefore get \(du = -\sin({{CT:0}})\,dv\). Hence: \[ dv = -\frac{du}{\sin({{CT:0}})}. \]
 So the integral becomes:
 \[\begin{array}{rcl}\displaystyle
 \int {{CT:3}}\,dv &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  \int e^u \cdot \sin({{CT:0}}) \cdot -\frac{du}{\sin({{CT:0}})}, \\
 &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  - \int e^u \,du, \\
 &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  -e^u + constant ,\\
 &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  -e^{\cos({{CT:0}})} + c.
  \end{array}\]
